title: Windows 11 gets November update with search and face login fixes
text:
Microsoft has released an optional update for Windows 11 that improves search speed and helps facial recognition work in dark rooms.

Microsoft has released a new optional update for Windows 11. This update, known as KB5132057, is available for versions 25H2 and 26H2. It includes 28 changes and fixes to make the system run better.

One key change is to Windows Search. The search box now has a cleaner design and removes promotional content from web results. This makes the tool more efficient and easier to use. You can also complete tasks like turning on dark mode directly from the search bar.

The update also improves Windows Hello, the facial recognition feature. If you enable a specific setting, your computer can now recognise your face in dark rooms. This helps you sign in more easily when the lights are off.

Microsoft says this is the final non-security preview update for the year. Normal monthly updates will resume in January. The company also warned that some devices might restart one extra time during installation to update security certificates.

title: Ruby programming language fixes security flaw
text:
A fix is available for a weakness in Ruby that could allow attackers to disrupt services, though experts say it is hard to exploit.

The Ruby programming language has released updates to fix seven security weaknesses. The most serious issue, called Ruby2Shell, involves a mistake in how the software handles text. This error could potentially let an attacker run commands on a server.

According to SecurityWeek, the flaw occurs when changing the capitalisation of letters in certain text formats. For example, turning a specific German character into uppercase might cause the software to write data in the wrong place in memory. This could corrupt the system.

Experts from WatchTowr told SecurityWeek that successfully using this flaw to take over a system is very difficult. They said attackers would need very specific conditions to be met. It is more likely that bad requests would just stop the service from working, rather than giving hackers full control.

Patches for all seven issues are included in Ruby versions 4.0.10, 3.4.13, or 3.3.14. The developers advise users to apply these fixes as soon as possible to stay safe.

title: F5 issues emergency fixes for critical security flaws
text:
A major US tech firm has released urgent updates to fix serious weaknesses in its network equipment, which could allow criminals to take control of systems.

US cybersecurity company F5 has warned customers to install emergency patches for five critical security flaws in its BIG-IP products. These weaknesses, known as remote code execution (RCE) flaws, allow attackers to run harmful commands on the device without needing a login. F5 said these issues are rated as critical severity.

The company also released a fix for a high-severity flaw that could cause the system to crash, a problem known as a denial-of-service (DoS) attack. F5 stated it has no other way to protect these systems besides installing the new updates. It advised security teams to apply the hotfixes released on Wednesday to vulnerable devices.

While F5 has not confirmed that these specific flaws are being used in attacks right now, it noted that cybercriminals and state-backed groups have often abused similar F5 vulnerabilities in the past. The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has previously flagged other F5 flaws as actively exploited. Therefore, F5 recommends upgrading systems to the latest version as soon as possible.

title: Microsoft now auto-installs Windows 11 26H2 on home PCs
text:
Microsoft is automatically upgrading eligible personal computers to the latest Windows 11 version, so you may see the update without checking for it yourself.

Microsoft has started automatically installing Windows 11 26H2 on devices that are not managed by an IT department. This includes personal computers and business devices that do not have central IT control.

The update is rolling out to devices currently running Windows 11 24H2 or 25H2. Microsoft said this step makes it easier for users to get the latest version without manual intervention.

You can still choose to install the update yourself. To do this, go to Settings, then Windows Update, and select 'Check for Windows updates'. You can also turn on the option to get the latest updates as soon as they are available.

Microsoft confirmed that this month's security update for newer Windows 11 versions is causing some issues with installing or launching Office and other apps. The company is aware of these problems.

title: New tactic: delivery photo upload failure to steal your parcel
text:
Criminals are using a new trick to steal parcels by claiming a photo upload failed, leaving shoppers to fight for refunds.

Reports of parcel theft in the UK have nearly doubled in a year. A Freedom of Information request by parcel firm Quadient found 12,802 reports in the year to June, up from 6,851 the previous year. The true number is likely higher because not all police forces provided data and many crimes go unreported.

Which? has heard reports of a new tactic. A delivery driver takes a picture of your doorstep as proof of delivery. They then claim the image cannot be uploaded due to a technical problem. They take the parcel back, promising to redeliver it later. In reality, the parcel is marked as delivered, making it hard to get a refund.

There are also reports of drivers taking a photo of a front door and driving off without getting out of the van. One man, Jon Barnes, reportedly found his Amazon locker empty. He took a photo as evidence, but Amazon initially refused a refund and threatened to close his account. He later received a reimbursement after contacting Which? and police.

Consumer law says the retailer must prove safe delivery. However, in practice, you may need to provide evidence that a parcel was missing. Staffed collection points, like post offices, offer a human witness, which can help if a parcel goes missing.

title: Careers360 data breach
text:
Data allegedly taken from the Indian education and careers platform Careers360 appeared on a public hacking forum.

In November 2026, data allegedly taken from the Indian education and careers platform Careers360 appeared on a public hacking forum. The 22M records included 3.6M unique email addresses alongside names, phone numbers, genders and caste categories, and most also contained students' entrance exam results, including ranks and marks.

The breach was added to the Have I Been Pwned database on 20 November 2026. The source attributes the incident to a threat actor known as 'Threat Actor 888'.

title: Why storing work passwords in spreadsheets is risky
text:
Spreadsheets often miss new or changed passwords, leaving companies unaware of weak or shared logins that attackers can exploit.

The password spreadsheet your admins use may look like a complete inventory, but it only reflects some of the credentials employees have reported using. More specifically, that spreadsheet doesn’t show passwords that have been changed, created, or shared since the document was last updated, until someone brings it up to date. That’s assuming someone ever does.

People often use easier methods to save passwords when official processes are slow. They might save logins in their web browser, send them in chat messages, or write them on sticky notes. A report by NordPass found that "123456" is the most common password used in a corporate setting. This shows that many people take the easy route when choosing passwords.

If a spreadsheet is out of date, it creates blind spots. Attackers who break into a company network often search for files with names like "password" or "login". If they find a spreadsheet, they can use the details inside to access other accounts. This can help them spread the attack further across the company.

To fix this, organisations need a better way to manage credentials. A business password manager provides a secure, central place to store work logins. It allows managers to see who has access to which accounts and check if passwords are weak or reused. This helps them spot problems early and keep company data safer.

title: Ofcom lists four ways to check if you are 16 for social media ban
text:
Ofcom has published a report identifying four reliable methods social media firms can use to verify users are over 16, ahead of the UK's upcoming ban.

Ofcom has published a rapid assessment on how social media companies can reliably determine if a user is aged 16 or over. This comes ahead of the UK Government setting out the practical rules for a social media ban for under-16s, which is expected to come into force next year.

The regulator identified four methods that are capable of being 'highly effective' at this age. These are photo ID matching, digital ID services, banking-based checks, and facial age estimation. Photo ID matching compares a document like a passport or driving licence to a live photo of the user. Banking checks use information held by a financial institution, while digital ID services allow people to prove their age online without repeatedly showing physical documents.

Facial age estimation uses technology to analyse a user's face to estimate their age. Because this method has a margin of error, Ofcom suggests it should be used alongside a second check, similar to how shops use 'Challenge 25' when selling alcohol. Ofcom notes that some 16 and 17-year-olds may need to obtain a photo ID to use these methods.

Ofcom says that while some children may still find ways to bypass these checks, the measures should significantly reduce the likelihood of under-16s accessing restricted sites. The regulator will monitor these attempts and publish research within twe

title: Ofcom investigates Meta over Instagram feature launch
text:
The UK regulator is checking if Meta broke safety laws by launching a new Instagram feature without assessing risks to children.

Ofcom has opened a formal investigation into Meta. The regulator wants to know if the company failed to follow UK online safety laws.

In May, Meta launched a feature called Instants on Instagram. This allows users to share content that disappears after it has been viewed. Under the UK’s Online Safety Act, tech firms must check for risks before making big changes to their services.

Ofcom says providers must assess how their features might expose children to harmful material. They also must check for risks of illegal content. The regulator warned earlier this year that firms could face action if they skipped these checks.

George Lusty, Director of Enforcement at Ofcom, compared the process to testing a new car. He said safety must be built in from the start, not added later. If the investigation finds a breach, Ofcom can order fixes or impose fines of up to £18 million or 10% of global revenue.

title: PHP updates fix 18 security flaws, including critical bugs
text:
The PHP team has released updates to fix 18 security issues, some of which could let attackers control servers.

The team that develops PHP, a popular tool for building websites, has released new security updates. These updates fix 18 different flaws in the software.

Some of these flaws are described as critical. This means an attacker could potentially run code on a server without needing to log in first. This is known as remote code execution.

According to the report, the updates were released on Thursday, 19 November. They are available for all supported versions of PHP, including the latest releases.

The updates are designed to close these gaps before they can be used to harm websites or servers.

title: WhatsApp fixes flaw that may have been used to make scam messages look real
text:
WhatsApp has fixed a security gap that scammers may have used to make their messages appear more trustworthy on Android phones.

WhatsApp has patched a low-impact flaw in its Android apps. The company says it found the issue while disrupting a scam campaign. A WhatsApp spokesperson told SecurityWeek that they believe a scammer was using it to make their scam message seem more credible.

The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-23871, is linked to 'Click to WhatsApp' ads. It affects both WhatsApp and WhatsApp Business for Android. If a specific type of ad message was displayed, it could have revealed your IP address (your device's unique internet location) to an attacker.

WhatsApp also fixed two other medium-impact issues. One bug could have allowed an attacker to delete WhatsApp files if you tapped a malicious 'order details' message from an unofficial app. The other involved a security check for Meta AI. WhatsApp says there is no evidence that either of these was exploited.

The company has released updates to fix all three problems.

title: Bell Canada confirms data breach affecting business customers
text:
A Canadian telecoms firm says a hacker stole business contact details, but says no personal passwords or sensitive files were taken.

Bell Canada has confirmed that its systems were breached on 17 November 2026. The company says an "agentic" threat actor accessed its networks. This term suggests the attacker used AI-powered tools to carry out the attack.

According to Bell, the hacker stole data from a system used to order and set up telephone connections. The information may have been stolen includes business contact details, such as names, job titles, and work email addresses. It also includes some technical details about network connections.

Bell told BleepingComputer that the data did not contain passwords, highly sensitive personal information, or file attachments. The company said it quickly secured its systems and that customer services have not been affected.

Bell has not said how many businesses were affected or who is responsible for the attack. It is sharing security details with the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security to help other organisations check for similar threats.

title: Singapore YMCA portal hit by data breach
text:
The YMCA of Singapore says its online application system was breached, exposing some personal details.

The YMCA of Singapore has confirmed a cybersecurity breach. It affected the online portal for its Youth For Causes programme. The organisation announced this on Saturday, 21 November 2026.

The breach involved the database linked to the application portal. This database held personal information about users. Some of this data included full or partial NRIC numbers.

The YMCA sent an email to participants and mentors on Saturday.

title: Microsoft fixes flaw that exposed business contact details
text:
Microsoft has fixed a security flaw in its Entra Connect Health service that allowed attackers to view some business contact details.

Microsoft says it found a weakness in its Entra Connect Health service on 9 November 2026. This service allows administrators to monitor the health, performance, and alerts of their on-premises identity infrastructure through the Microsoft Entra admin centre. Attackers used this weakness to look at certain information about companies.

The company confirmed that attackers could see email addresses for technical contacts and administrators. They could also see basic details like company names and country codes. Microsoft says it did not find any evidence that attackers changed any settings or stole passwords.

Microsoft fixed the problem on 19 November 2026. It has now told affected businesses about the issue. The company has not said how many businesses were affected or who the attackers were.

Microsoft advises businesses to be careful. It warns that scammers might use the exposed email addresses to send fake messages. These messages, known as phishing, try to trick people into giving away more details.

title: Rackspace Spot breach exposed customer cloud secrets
text:
Hackers used stolen login details to access a cloud platform, potentially exposing sensitive passwords and keys for business customers.

Rackspace has warned that hackers breached its Rackspace Spot cloud platform. The company said attackers used leaked credentials to access parts of the system on 17 November 2026. This allowed them to act like legitimate users in some customer organisations.

The attackers could create new workloads and read 'Kubernetes Secrets'. These are secure files that store sensitive information such as passwords, authentication tokens, and API keys. Rackspace warned that the hackers could have read any secret stored in an affected user's clusters.

Rackspace says it learned of the intrusion on 18 November after a customer report. The company has since revoked affected tokens, removed unauthorised workloads, and rotated keys. It also strengthened access controls and monitoring to prevent further issues.

The breach caused an extended outage of the Rackspace Spot administration console. This temporarily prevented customers from managing their clusters. Service was fully restored on 21 November 2026.

title: Michigan nurse jailed for Medicare fraud using stolen records
text:
A nurse in the US was sentenced to prison for billing Medicare for services that never happened, using stolen patient details.

Ruby Scott, a nurse from Farmington Hills, Michigan, has been sentenced to four years in federal prison. She owned a home health care company called Delta Home Health Care LLC. According to a press release from the Justice Department, she used stolen patient records to bill Medicare for fake services. The total value of the fraud scheme was reported as $1.6 million. Fox2 in Detroit reported that the sentencing took place on Thursday.

title: Criminals use phone calls to steal data from businesses
text:
A security firm says criminals are using phone calls to steal data.

Unit 42, a security team, has tracked several waves of attacks in recent months. These attacks are called vishing. This is a type of scam where criminals use phone calls to steal data.

The group behind these calls is linked to Com. Unit 42 says these attacks have led to data theft and attempts to demand money. The criminals targeted companies in industries that hold lots of personal data. This includes financial services, healthcare and legal services.

The main goal was to steal data and then use it for extortion.

This story is important because it shows how phone calls can be dangerous.

title: Cleverbridge breach exposes payment card details
text:
Cleverbridge says hackers stole payment card details, including security codes, from its online sales platform.

Cleverbridge is an online service that helps software companies sell products and process payments. The company says it detected unauthorised activity on 4 November 2026. It temporarily took its systems offline to contain the breach.

Cleverbridge confirmed that a third party copied payment card data. A notification sent to customers reveals that the stolen information includes card numbers, expiry dates, and CVV codes.

The company says it did not steal other personal data, such as names or billing addresses. It has not said how many customers were affected or how the attackers got in. Cleverbridge has told data protection authorities and law enforcement about the incident.

The company is working with TransUnion to send out notifications. It is also offering free credit monitoring to affected customers to help them track their accounts.

title: Phone company fined £437,500 for letting scammers use its numbers
text:
Ofcom has fined Tismi for failing to stop scammers from using phone numbers it provided, putting consumers at risk of fraud.

Ofcom has fined telecoms provider Tismi £437,500. The regulator found that Tismi failed to take proper steps to prevent its phone numbers from being misused by scammers. This failure lasted from November 2022 to January 2025. During this time, approximately 366,000 numbers were exposed to potential misuse.

Phone companies must check their business customers to stop scammers getting valid numbers. They must also monitor for misuse and handle reports properly. Ofcom found that Tismi did not carry out these checks or have the right systems in place. It also lacked a formal process for dealing with reports of misuse.

Ofcom Director of Enforcement George Lusty said there is no excuse for failing to put proper checks in place. He stated that companies putting customers at the mercy of scammers will face consequences. The fine will be passed to HM Treasury. Tismi received a 30% discount on the fine because it admitted liability.

As part of the decision, Tismi must now prove it is following the rules. It must provide details of its new checks and monitoring processes. Ofcom has also opened a new investigation into another company, Xtra Phones UK, over similar concerns about number misuse.

title: Ofcom warns about 'job offer' and missed call phone scams
text:
Criminals are using automated voices and quick hang-ups to trick you into calling back, so you should hang up and report these calls.

Ofcom has warned the public about two common types of scam phone calls. One uses an automated voice to claim you have a job offer. The other is a call from an unknown number that hangs up after just a few moments.

These calls are designed to make you call the number back. Once you are on the line, criminals try to pressure you into giving away sensitive personal details or making payments to accounts they control. You could also accidentally call a premium-rate number and run up a large bill.

Ofcom says the number of people reporting suspicious calls has fallen over the last four years. However, the regulator is still investigating four telecoms providers as part of its ongoing work to tackle phone scams.

An Ofcom spokesperson said: “Tackling this complex problem requires a joined-up approach from Government, other regulators, law enforcement and industry.” They noted that telecoms companies are already blocking millions of scam calls every month.
